claims.label: CORRECT

claims.label: CORRECT
claims.note: All quotes verified. The 20-query set was the starting eval set, so 'eval set was ~20 queries' is a slight over-reading.

claims.claim: Scaling Agent Systems: 260 configs, six benchmarks, three LLM families, matched token budgets; +80.8% to -70.0%; ~45% threshold; error amplification 17.2x vs 4.4x
claims.label: MINOR_ERROR
claims.note: Mixes two versions. The abs page says 260 configs / six benchmarks / standardized compute, with no 45% or 17.2x. The HTML says 180 configs / four benchmarks / matched token budgets / 45% / 17.2x / 4.4x. Every number appears somewhere in the cited sources, but the combined description matches neither version.

claims.claim: Tran & Kiela: SAS 'consistently match or outperform' MAS on multi-hop reasoning at equal reasoning tokens; gains from 'unaccounted computation and context effects'; API budget-control artifacts
claims.label: CORRECT
claims.note: Quotes verified.

claims.label: MINOR_ERROR

claims.label: CORRECT

claims.label: CORRECT

claims.label: CORRECT
claims.note: Verified.

P.summary: This is the broadest and most precise report. Almost every claim rests on a primary source, and it clearly separates the no-tools baseline from the tool-equipped single-agent baseline. It surfaces the compute confound, vendor vs independent evals, task-type and horizon dependence, and agents' citation-accuracy deficit. It has two small blemishes: it blends two versions of the scaling paper (260 configs vs 180 configs) and it gives an unverified NeurIPS venue for MAST. Its one secondary source (Nature coverage) is honestly flagged.

claims.claim: Anthropic 90.2% (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents); multi-agent ~15x vs agent ~4x chat tokens, so ~3.75x per task; 80% of BrowseComp variance from tokens
claims.label: CORRECT
claims.note: Verified. The 3.75x is a reasonable derivation.

claims.note: All verified (MAST v3 has 1600+ traces).

Q.summary: Every claim I checked is accurate, all citations resolve to the right papers, and it adds distinctive nuance (the HLE text-only subset, DeepTRACE citation reliability). But it is thin. Several sources were read only at abstract level, by its own admission, and findings are compressed with little quantitative detail on task-type or scaffold effects. It gives a decision-maker the right headline but fewer actionable specifics than P or R.

claims.claim: Anthropic 90.2%; ~15x chat tokens; tokens explain 80% of BrowseComp variance
claims.label: CORRECT
claims.note: Verified.

claims.claim: MLE-bench: pass@8 vs pass@1 doubles score; best setup 16.9% bronze+; GPT-4o AIDE 8.7% vs OpenHands 4.4% vs MLAB 0.8%
claims.label: CORRECT
claims.note: 16.9% -> 34.1%; scaffold numbers match.

claims.claim: Equal-inference-cost study: evolved team 0.769 vs 0.754 on ALFWorld/WebShop, not significant; 1.02x ratio; 7B backbone
claims.label: MINOR_ERROR
claims.note: 0.769 vs 0.754 is ALFWorld only (WebShop: no effect, team trends worse). The 1.02x ratio is derived, not reported. The conclusion is intact.

claims.label: CORRECT
claims.note: Correctly flags the 180/260 version discrepancy. The blog says 80.9%, the paper 80.8%.

claims.label: CORRECT

claims.label: CORRECT

claims.claim: Unscaffolded long-context model matches tuned scaffolds on SWE-bench Verified (38% vs 32%)
claims.label: CORRECT

claims.claim: Sakana AI Scientist: 42% of experiments failed from coding errors (independent eval); AI Scientist-v2: 1 of 3 workshop submissions cleared the threshold, none met the internal main-track bar
claims.label: CORRECT
claims.note: Verified.

R.summary: Very strong and fully primary-sourced. Its distinctive, decision-relevant findings are that pure compute (pass@8) matches scaffold gains on MLE-bench, that scaffold effects depend on the model, and that an unscaffolded long-context model matches tuned scaffolds. It explicitly flags the 180/260 discrepancy in the scaling paper. Its only slip attributes the ALFWorld 0.769/0.754 result to ALFWorld and WebShop together. It is marginally behind P on breadth (no HAL, no RE-Bench detail, and the no-tools vs tool-equipped baseline distinction is less explicit).
